findings.issue_text: config is normalized to the schedule-type display value, but returned context uses monitor_environment.monitor.config, exposing the raw schedule type instead
Threshold check-ins queried with .values() are loaded again by ID, causing an unnecessary database query for every incident occurrence

goldens.comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
per_golden_matches.matched_candidate: config is normalized to the schedule-type display value, but returned context uses monitor_environment.monitor.config, exposing the raw schedule type instead
per_golden_matches.reasoning: Both comments identify the same issue: the code modifies a 'config' variable to include display values (normalizing schedule-type), but then returns monitor.config (the original/raw version) instead of the modified config variable. The golden comment says it 'returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version' and the candidate says 'returned context uses monitor_environment.monitor.config, exposing the raw schedule type instead'. These are describing the exact same bug.

per_golden_matches.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.
per_golden_matches.matched_candidate: Threshold check-ins queried with .values() are loaded again by ID, causing an unnecessary database query for every incident occurrence
per_golden_matches.reasoning: The candidate issue identifies the same problem as the golden comment - that check-ins are being queried/loaded again by ID when the data already exists from a previous query (the .values() query that populated previous_checkins). Both comments point out the unnecessary database query caused by fetching MonitorCheckIn objects when the required data is already available.
